title: Population Dynamics
standard_text: Population size, density and distribution; birth, death, immigration and emigration; exponential and logistic growth; carrying capacity and limiting factors; interactions between species; and the human population and sustainability. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Biology, Grade 12, University Preparation (SBI4U), Strand F: Population Dynamics)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Biology (SBI4U) worksheets on population dynamics: density, mark–recapture, growth rates, exponential and logistic growth, carrying capacity, species interactions and the human population. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Logistic growth levels off at the carrying capacity.
body_html:
How to think about it

Population density = number of individuals ÷ area. The mark–recapture estimate is N = (number marked × number caught the second time) ÷ number recaptured with marks. A population grows when births and immigration are greater than deaths and emigration.

With unlimited resources, a population grows exponentially (a J-shaped curve). Limiting factors such as food, space and disease slow growth, giving a logistic, S-shaped curve that levels off at the carrying capacity. Density-dependent factors (competition, disease) get stronger as the population grows.

Example

50 deer are tagged. Later 40 are caught and 10 have tags. Estimate the population.

N = 50 × 40 ÷ 10

Answer: 200 deer

Example

A town of 2000 has 60 births, 20 deaths, 10 immigrants and 30 emigrants in a year. Change?

(60 + 10) − (20 + 30)

Answer: +20

Common mistakes

  • Thinking carrying capacity never changes: it changes when the environment does.
  • Calling a predator–prey relationship mutualism.
  • Forgetting immigration and emigration in population change.

faq.q: Why do predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles?
faq.a: More prey feeds more predators; more predators then reduce the prey, so the predators fall too.

items.q: Noah needs an example of competition (organisms need the same limited resource). Which is the best example?
c: oxpecker birds eat ticks off zebras
fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water
mistletoe takes water and nutrients from a tree
two kinds of birds eat the same insects
items.e: That is competition.

items.q: Hana observes that fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In mutualism, both benefit.

items.q: Arjun needs an example of mutualism (both benefit). Which is the best example?

items.e: That is mutualism.

items.q: Lucas needs an example of commensalism (one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed). Which is the best example?

a mosquito feeds on a person's blood

items.e: That is commensalism.
